newsitem.title: USA: Steady US rates should fuel booming junk bond mart.
newsitem.headline: Steady US rates should fuel booming junk bond mart.

text.p: The Federal Reserve's decision to hold interest rates steady should extend the spectacular run U.S. high-yield corporate bonds have racked up so far in 1996, dealers and analysts said on Tuesday.
Hybrids of debt and equity securities, junk bonds thrive when the economy grows fast enough to boost company creditworthiness but not enough to prompt a sharp jump in interest rates.

"It is the ideal environment for high-yield bonds because people aren't afraid of the hammer (recession) coming down," said Walter McGuire, associate director at Bear, Stearns & Co Inc, speaking of the current economic climate after the Federal Open Market Committee left interest rates unchanged.
"The high-yield market is very comfortable with the economy moving out slightly better than people expected."
Favorable monetary conditions coupled with strong technicals have made 1996 a banner year for junk investors, even in the face of possible short-term rate hikes.

High-yield bonds rallied amid a slump in Treasuries last week. AMG Data Services reported a $562 million inflow into high-yield mutual funds in the week ending September 18, double the year-to-date weekly average. That contrasted with an unspectacular inflow into taxable bond funds, said Merrill Lynch high-yield research.

"The (junk bond) market has very strong technicals. Cash inflow versus supply is extremely robust. I think the relative value of high-yield is nothing short of spectacular," said Sameh DeRosa-Farag, head of high-yield portfolio and strategic research at Chase Securities Inc.
He said that on a relative basis, high-yield markets now retain more upside and less downside than U.S. equities and will give higher returns than Treasuries.
Noninvestment-grade notes outperformed 10-year Treasuries by nearly 1,000 basis points on a nonannualized basis during the first eight months of this year, analysts said.

The spread between 10-year junk notes and Treasuries stands at 289 basis points, a smidgen above the smallest differential observed since the beginning of 1992, which was 282 basis points on April 4, 1994, according to Merrill Lynch.

"The only thing you have to look at is will there be a recession. As long as you avoid the blow ups, you'll be okay," Bear Stearns' McGuire said, adding he doubts spreads will widen more than 20 basis points regardless of Fed policy.
High-yield analysts do not fear a possible rate hike at the next Federal Open Market Committee meeting on November 13.

Some experts said speculative-grade debt may even benefit from tighter monetary policy in the short-term as junk bonds are perceived as a more attractive investment vehicle on a relative basis than interest-rate sensitive U.S. Treasuries and high-grade corporate bonds.
"The short-run impact of a 25 basis point rise in rates would probably be, on a relative basis, beneficial for high yield," said Martin Fridson, high-yield global strategist at Merrill Lynch & Co.
"The immediate response would be that (spreads) will tighten," he added.
Analysts see robust market technicals outweighing any looming risk of a deterioration in credit quality if U.S. economic growth gets squeezed by higher rates.
"(A Fed rate hike) is not going to trigger a reversal in demand of this asset class at this point," McGuire said.
